topic: Foundations of Linear Algebra: From Span to Basis

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresh: Vectors as Arrows
sections.content: Briefly define vectors as directed quantities in 2D space. Explain that we can scale them (scalar multiplication) and connect them head-to-tail (vector addition).
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Robot Arm' in 2D: Two segments that can stretch and rotate to reach any point.

sections.title: Linear Combinations and Span
sections.content: Define a linear combination as adding scaled vectors (c1v1 + c2v2). Define 'Span' as the collection of all possible points reachable through these combinations. Use a grid animation to show how two non-parallel vectors sweep across the 2D plane.
sections.example: If a squirrel can jump in vector v1 and vector v2, the 'Span' is the entire territory the squirrel can reach in the park.

sections.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Vector
sections.content: Explain linear dependence as the existence of 'redundancy'. If one vector lies on the line of another, it adds no new reach. Visually show a vector shrinking to zero or overlapping, indicating it can be 'represented' by others.
sections.example: Three delivery drones where one drone's path is just the sum of the other two; the third drone is 'linearly dependent' and unnecessary for the mission.

sections.title: The Concept of a Basis
sections.content: Define a Basis as the 'minimalist' set: vectors that span the space without any redundancy (linearly independent). Explain that every vector in the space can be represented by a unique set of coordinates using the basis.
sections.example: A GPS coordinate system: The unit vectors 'East' and 'North' serve as the basis. Every location on the map is just a unique linear combination of these two.

sections.title: Summary & Visualization
sections.content: Recap: Span (reach), Linear Dependence (overlap), and Basis (efficient coordinate system). Show a 3D animation where removing a dependent vector collapses a volume into a plane, demonstrating why bases are essential for defining dimensions.
sections.example: An architect designing a room: The basis vectors are the corners of the floor; if the vectors aren't independent, the room collapses into a flat line!
